First I think its important to acknowledge that FOMO exists. Every trader, regardless of whether you are new or seasoned - experiences FOMO to varying degrees.

The difference is in knowing what happens over a large dataset when you succumb to FOMO.

@Kluts4 @TraderLion This is a tough one, and a great question! Honestly something I still struggle with (though much better compared to earlier years).

The difficulty isn't because you can't sit out of a choppy environment, its exponentially increased because the market eggs you enough to keep you engaged enough just to rug you, toiling on your mental capital until the real turn comes and you're too exhausted to engage again.

My solution thus far: 

(1) Think very deep about your trading system: 

When are you allowed to be aggressive and chase for opening range entries? When are you not allowed to and should only engage 30-minutes after the market open?

Which type of entry styles (breakouts or pullbacks) favor a choppy market environment? Within each entry style, what is the entry tactic? (5-min 6/20 MACD turns, or 30-min pullback pivots, etc...)

What type of profit taking rules should you have in a chop market? (say take half position off at 3R instead of 1/3 in trending environments).

How many new trades are you allowed per day? Max risk per session?

Importantly: What is your A+ setup? What filtering criteria do you have that differentiates this setup vs the rest? (In choppy markets, you won't find that many A+ setups).

Having this clarity allows you to engage a chop market without doing too much damage to the account.

(2) The next part of this is situational awareness: How do market cycles start? You will have conduct deep dives to find the answer to this. This article may help!

@_mohitkhanna_ @TraderLion Good question! I would like to first have you read this quote that I got from 'Trend Following' by Michael Covel:

"Trends develop because there’s an accumulating consensus on future prices, consequently there’s an evolution to the true price value over time. Because investors/traders are human and they make mistakes, they’re never 100% sure of their vision and whether or not their view is correct.   

So price adjustments take time as they fluctuate and a new consensus is formed in the face of changing market conditions and new facts.   

For some changes, this consensus is easy to reach, but there are other events that take time to formulate a market view. It’s those events that take time that form the basis of profits." - John W Henry

In relation to your question (answering from the lens of a William O'Neil type growth stock trader), clean breakouts can occur under the context of post-market corrections because positioning has been reset - everyone has hopped off the boat and no one has exposure. So what happens? They chase stocks higher to get their desired allocation.

As the rally lengthens in duration, most have already gotten exposure, trades get crowded, that's when you likely want to focus on just pullback buying because trends are an accumulating consensus on future prices.

Now the other scenario where breakouts will work is in a manic, hot market environment. You will see the most speculative issues form beautiful technical patterns and breaking out. In my memory, we last saw that in October 2025 with the strategic rare earth/mineral names.

Hope that answers your question!

@GuyTheInvestor @TraderLion Great question Guy!

(1) From the perspective of a swing/position trader, it helps to have a general idea of whether you're early in a cycle or late in a cycle. 

During the earlier parts of the cycle, you ideally want to trim less of the initial position (to derisk it if that's part of your process), and let the balance trail via the 10-MA or 20-MA (again dependent on your process).

On this, it helps to study how the biggest stock market winners of the past and how they setup, move out, stall/top out, and break their MAs. This builds muscle memory to know what you can expect from your positions.

Now when we get to a later part of the cycle, the uptrend has gone on for a certain duration, you now likely want to sell newer positions into strength more frequently. Setups are few and far between, price action gets choppy, and you will likely find it difficult to gain traction. This is where it becomes harder to hold winners.

(2) In protecting your equity curve, you have to heed feedback from your trades. The magic is when you pair that feedback with situational awareness. If you are beginning to see warning signs, like leaders breaking down hard, and the feedback of your last 5 trades were losers - that's a sign to dial it back on the risk taking.

(3) Following rules is hard for sure! I break rules sometimes too and suffer the consequences.

I think the key is in deciding which is more painful:

(1) Following rules and missing a trade, or stopping out on a trade.

or 

(2) Breaking rules and having that become a habit.

When the pain of staying the same (breaking rules) outweigh the pain of making the change, you will change!

If you've found yourself breaking rules, don't be discouraged - we all do from time to time. The key is in acknowledging the mistake, letting it go, and finding the courage to be disciplined again!

A good reminder to have a strategy, understand it and deploy it efficiently.

@ThePAVTrader @TraderLion Good question! You're on the right track in thinking that I try to adapt to market conditions.

I usually like to start every year with a clean slate. So with 0% YTD PnL, I'm trying to go for base hits, easy trades - things that can move my equity curve up as I build cushion.

When I get beyond a certain point (say 20% YTD PnL) AND I see that market conditions are starting to favor my trading style, I will get aggressive as long as the positions I take are showing me traction. 

To quote Stanley Druckenmiller:

“I see a lot of managers to get up 20% or 'I want to book my year. I made my high watermark. Let's go to the beach.' I'm the opposite... If you're up 20 or 30%, you're playing in the house money, that's when you try and get up 60 or 70% and you're usually...”

and to also quote Victor Sperandeo, you always want to approach your trading business with the three principles in mind, one after the other:

1) Preservation of Capital
2) Consistent Profitability, and
3) Pursuit of Superior Returns

SO, once I've knocked it out of the park, say 50% YTD and the market conditions really are rewarding me, I shouldn't stop because this could be THE year to make big returns. In that case, I'm okay to suffer a larger drawdown from equity curve peak because of the 'house money' mindset. 

For me, I am okay trading off 20-25% off my peak because my worst case scenario is I have a decent year, but my best case scenario is I knock it out of the park!

1 easy way I’ve found to stop fighting the market is to ask a stupidly simple question every morning:

Is this a green, yellow, or red light environment?

I have a few different ways I judge the environment (individual stock PA, breadth, leadership, my own P&L/feedback loop, watchlist length, etc.), but if someone wanted the simplest framework possible, I’d start with the indices: $SPY, $QQQ & $IWM.

And the funny thing is, you really don’t need much more than 2 moving averages to get a surprisingly useful answer.

1) GREEN LIGHT = good weather.

I want to see the index above a rising 21EMA, with the 9EMA > the 21EMA and price generally making constructive HH/HLs.

That tells me the short-term trend has the wind at its back. In this environment, I’m much more comfortable buying breakouts/ORBs, holding for larger moves, progressively adding exposure as positions work, and potentially using more size. Think of it like driving on a dry highway: I’m still wearing my seatbelt, but I’m comfortable pressing the gas because conditions allow it.

2) YELLOW LIGHT = conflicting information.

Maybe price is above the 21EMA, but it’s flat. Maybe the 9/21EMAs are crossing back and forth, price keeps chopping through them, or the index is stuck in a range with no sustained follow-through. This is where I’ve learned to stop forcing “green-light trades” in a yellow-light environment.

I’ll reduce size, become WAY more selective, favor entries closer to support/invalidation rather than blindly chasing breakouts, take profits quicker when appropriate, and generally demand better R/R. If every breakout goes +5% and round-trips, eventually I have to stop blaming the stocks and realize the weather sucks!

3) RED LIGHT = capital preservation mode.

If the index is below a declining 21EMA, especially with the 9EMA underneath it and price producing LL/LHs, I have very little interest in aggressively pressing longs. 

Breakouts become lower quality to me, failed moves become more common, and my priority shifts from making money to keeping money. I’ll aggressively reduce exposure, sit mostly in cash when necessary, and if shorting is part of the plan, I can flip the same framework upside down. I don’t need to prove that I can make money every single day while the wind is blowing directly into my face.

The important nuance is that green doesn’t mean BUY EVERYTHING and red doesn’t mean SELL EVERYTHING. 

This is a framework for determining how much aggression the environment deserves, not some magical indicator that predicts tomorrow. A great leader can show RS during a red-light environment, and I absolutely want to track that because it may become one of the first names I attack when conditions improve. 

Likewise, a garbage stock doesn’t magically become an A+ trade because QQQ is above its 21EMA.

I look at plenty of other evidence...breadth, groups, individual leaders, relative strength, price/volume, how breakouts are behaving, and probably most importantly, whether my own trades/setups are actually paying me quickly. But I think traders sometimes add 37 variables before they’ve learned to read the speedometer.

Start stupidly simple:

- above a rising 21EMA with 9 > 21 = green
- conflicting/flat = yellow
- below a declining 21EMA with 9 < 21 = red.

Learn how your setups behave under each light, then slowly add context from there...

Godspeed, family!

One of the Biggest Changes I Made to My Approach to the Market - And How It Helped Me Catch Multibaggers

I used to think I needed to wait for the breakout.

I don’t anymore.

Over time, I’ve learned that I much prefer building my positions inside the base rather than buying regular breakouts or chasing extended ones.

If I get the fundamentals right and the technical structure is developing the way I want, I’m comfortable getting positioned while the base is still forming.

I usually look for:
- A powerful long-term theme
- Accelerating fundamentals
- EPS growth above 30% yoy 
- Stage 1 base or consolidation
- Higher lows + signs of accumulation
- Support around key MAs / AVWAPs

This is where fundamentals and technicals work together for me. Fundamentals tell me what I want to own. Technicals tell me when I want to start building it.

By the time the breakout comes, I already want to have a position. I’m not looking at the breakout as my entry anymore - I look at it as confirmation.

Recent examples:
$HOOD around $105
$RBRK around $75

Past winners:
$ARM around $160
$MRVL around $92

I’m not trying to predict the exact bottom of the base. I’m trying to recognize when a great business is building a structure that could eventually lead to its next Stage 2 move.

And position sizing matters.

I don’t need to go full size on day one. I can start building inside the base and add as the technicals improve and the thesis continues to play out.

That’s one of the biggest advantages I’ve found from combining fundamentals + technicals.

But getting in early is only half of it.

The other side of this approach is holding my winners much longer.

Once a position breaks out and enters a strong Stage 2 trend, I don’t want to sell just because I’m up 30%, 50%, or even 100%.

I stay with the trend until something materially changes. And I never make that decision based on a single indicator. It’s always a combination of factors - price action, key MAs/AVWAPs, trend structure, distribution, and whether the fundamentals or original thesis have changed. One indicator breaking doesn’t automatically mean the trend is over.

Getting positioned inside the base gives me the cost basis.

Staying with the trend gives the position enough time to become a multibagger.

Find them early. Build inside the base. Add on confirmation. Hold while the trend remains intact.

$MRNA is about as textbook an example as I can find right now, and the clues were sitting there LONG before this latest leg higher.

$MRNA initially exploded higher on a catalyst and eventually ran roughly 177% off the lows. But the move itself isn’t what interests me most...it’s what happened after everyone got excited. Instead of immediately round-tripping the entire move, price spent multiple weeks digesting those gains.

The range gradually tightened, the 9EMA caught up, volume contracted, and sellers repeatedly failed to make any progress lower. That’s exactly what I want to see:

big expansion → boring digestion → compression.

Why does tightness matter so much to me? Because a stock moving violently in both directions tells me buyers + sellers are still fighting for control.

When the range starts contracting, and volume dries up, that fight is becoming increasingly one-sided because fewer holders are willing to sell at those prices. It’s almost like squeezing a spring...I don’t know which exact second it releases, but the tighter it gets, the more interested I become in the eventual expansion.

As a trader, that tightness also gives me something equally important: super duper defined risk!!

And $MRNA wasn’t perfect throughout the entire base that’s actually part of what makes this example useful. Price lost the 9EMA and could have easily rolled over, but sellers couldn’t capitalize. Buyers reclaimed the 9EMA, price tightened AGAIN, a mini-coil setup developed, and then buyers pushed through the prior high volume close on expanding volume. That’s a character change I care about.

A failed setup doesn’t mean I blacklist the stock...if price repairs itself and gives me another valid trigger, I’m perfectly happy buying it back.

Volume is the confirmation piece.

During digestion, I generally want to see volume contract because it suggests supply is drying up. When price finally leaves that range, I want the opposite: expanding price + increasing volume. That tells me buyers aren’t just poking their heads above resistance, but they’re showing up with actual demand.

$MRNA gave us exactly that as it pushed through the high volume pivot and started expanding toward the 200 psych area (my next target).

That’s why I spend so much time stalking prior leaders instead of searching for a brand new ticker every morning.

I watch for...

>catalyst/abnormal strength
>orderly digestion/volume contraction
>tightness/reclaim
>volume expansion
...potential next leg?

I don’t need every stock to check every box perfectly, but when several of those clues start stacking on top of each other, my job becomes pretty stupidly simple.

So the next time a stock makes a monster move, don’t automatically assume you missed it. Put it on a watchlist and study what happens when the excitement disappears.

If price stays tight, volume dries up, sellers stop making progress, key EMAs get reclaimed, and volume comes roaring back on the next breakout… pay attention.

$MRNA is a textbook example of why sometimes the best opportunity comes after everyone thinks the move already happened.

The best stress medicine in trading is having a proper cushion in your positions and across your portfolio.

And part of building that cushion is recognizing the little clues that can show up before a market turn becomes obvious: leaders holding up while the indexes struggle, fewer stocks making new lows, improving breadth, or setups finally starting to follow through.

Those clues give me a reason to start testing exposure early, with small positions and defined risk. There will be false starts. The idea is to see whether the market rewards those initial trades, then gradually build as the evidence improves.

By the time the strength becomes obvious to everyone, you may already have positions working and some breathing room. That feels very different from chasing extended stocks with full size because you suddenly feel left behind.

A cushion makes it easier to sit through normal pullbacks and give a trade time to develop. But open profits can disappear, and adding too aggressively can erase that comfort quickly.

Get involved early enough to build a cushion, keep the initial risk small enough to handle being wrong, and let follow-through earn the bigger exposure.

Where is the money flowing?
